items.stem: Which of the following statements about the centre of mass is correct?
items.answer: The centre of mass of a system moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted there.
items.markingKey: (a) Correct: "The centre of mass of a system moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted there." The other three are false.
options: The centre of mass of a system moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted there.
The centre of mass must always lie inside the material of the body.
Internal forces can accelerate the centre of mass of an isolated system.
The centre of mass of two particles is always at the midpoint between them.

items.stem: A person stands at one end of a boat floating on still water and walks to the other end. Why does the boat move?
items.answer: No external horizontal force acts, so the CM stays fixed; the boat moves backward as the person moves forward.
items.markingKey: CM of isolated system fixed (1 mark); boat moves opposite (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The centre of mass of a shell exploding in mid-air continues on its parabolic path.
Reason (R): The forces of the explosion are internal forces.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Two particles of masses 2 kg and 10 kg are placed 2 m apart. How far from the 2 kg particle is their centre of mass?
Three particles are placed in the x-y plane: 1 kg at (3, 2), 3 kg at (2, 5), 5 kg at (2, 2) (coordinates in metres). Find the coordinates of their centre of mass.

Gauri (mass 50 kg) stands at one end of a 3 m long boat of mass 250 kg at rest in still water. Gauri walks to the other end. How far does the boat move, and in which direction? (Neglect water resistance.)
items.markingKey: CM fixed: m(L − x) = Mx ⇒ x = mL/(m + M) = 50 × 3/300 = 0.500 m (2); boat moves backward (1).

items.stem: A 4 kg ball and a 5 kg ball are joined by a light rod 30 cm long. How far from the 5 kg ball is the centre of mass?
items.markingKey: Distance from the heavier ball = m₁d/(m₁ + m₂) = 4 × 30/9 = 13.3 cm.

items.stem: Why does the centre of mass of a ring lie at its centre, where there is no material?
items.answer: By symmetry, mass elements on opposite sides balance about the centre.
items.markingKey: Symmetry argument (2 marks).

items.stem: A shell fired from a gun would have landed 600 m away on level ground. At the highest point it explodes into two fragments with masses in the ratio 1 : 2. The lighter fragment falls vertically down. Where does the other fragment land?
items.markingKey: CM still lands at 600 m (1). First fragment lands at R/2 = 300 m (1). 1(R/2) + 2x = 3R ⇒ x = 750 m (2).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the centre of mass is NOT correct?
items.answer: The centre of mass of two particles is always at the midpoint between them.
items.markingKey: (c) "The centre of mass of two particles is always at the midpoint between them." is false; the other three are true.
options: The centre of mass of a system moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted there.
The centre of mass of a body need not lie within the body.
The centre of mass of two particles is always at the midpoint between them.
The centre of mass of a uniform rod is at its midpoint.

items.stem: A 2 kg ball and a 5 kg ball are joined by a light rod 90 cm long. How far from the 5 kg ball is the centre of mass?
items.markingKey: Distance from the heavier ball = m₁d/(m₁ + m₂) = 2 × 90/7 = 25.7 cm.

items.stem: Three particles are placed in the x-y plane: 1 kg at (5, 4), 4 kg at (6, 2), 5 kg at (2, 6) (coordinates in metres). Find the coordinates of their centre of mass.
Two particles of masses 5 kg and 2 kg are placed 3 m apart. How far from the 5 kg particle is their centre of mass?

Assertion (A): For two particles, the centre of mass lies closer to the heavier particle.
Reason (R): The distances of the particles from the centre of mass are inversely proportional to their masses.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) m₁r₁ = m₂r₂; R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the vector product is NOT correct?
items.markingKey: (c) "A × B = B × A." is false; the other three are true.
options: A × B = −B × A.
The vector product of two parallel vectors is zero.
A × B = B × A.
î × ĵ = k̂.

items.stem: Why is it easier to open a door by pushing at the handle (far from the hinges) than near the hinges?
items.answer: Torque = rF sin θ; a larger r gives the needed torque with a smaller force.
items.markingKey: Torque formula (1 mark); larger moment arm (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The torque of a force about a point on its line of action is zero.
Reason (R): The position vector r is parallel to F in that case.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) r × F = 0 for parallel vectors; R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A force of 10 N is applied at the end of a tap handle 15 cm from the axis, at 90° to the arm. Find the torque about the axis.
Find the torque τ = r × F of the force F = (2î + 3ĵ − 2k̂) N acting at the point r = (−4î − 2ĵ + 3k̂) m about the origin.
A wheel of radius 25 cm rotates at 900 rpm about a fixed axis. Find its angular velocity and the linear speed of a point on its rim.
For A = −3î − 1ĵ + 2k̂ and B = 0î − 1ĵ + 3k̂, find A × B, its magnitude, and hence the area of the parallelogram formed by A and B.
items.answer: A × B = −1î + 9ĵ + 3k̂; |A × B| = 9.54; area = 9.54 square units
items.markingKey: Expand the determinant (2): A × B = −1î + 9ĵ + 3k̂; magnitude √(1 + 81 + 9) = 9.54 (1); area of parallelogram = |A × B| (1).

items.stem: Why is the torque zero when the force passes through the axis of rotation?
items.answer: The moment arm (perpendicular distance from axis to line of force) is zero.
items.markingKey: τ = F × perpendicular distance (2 marks).

items.stem: The relation l = r × p gives the
items.markingKey: (d) angular momentum of a particle: l = r × p.
options: magnitude of a vector product
torque
linear velocity of a point on a rotating body
angular momentum of a particle

items.stem: A force of 50 N is applied at the end of a tap handle 30 cm from the axis, at 45° to the arm. Find the torque about the axis.
items.markingKey: τ = rF sin θ = 0.3 × 50 × sin 45° = 10.6 N m.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): î × ĵ = −k̂.
Reason (R): The unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ form a right-handed system.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false (î × ĵ = k̂); R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the vector product is correct?
items.answer: The vector product of two parallel vectors is zero.
items.markingKey: (a) Correct: "The vector product of two parallel vectors is zero." The other three are false.
options: The vector product of two parallel vectors is zero.
A × B lies in the plane of A and B.
A × B = B × A.

items.stem: The relation |A × B| = AB sin θ gives the
items.markingKey: (a) magnitude of a vector product: |A × B| = AB sin θ.
options: magnitude of a vector product
torque
angular momentum of a particle
linear velocity of a point on a rotating body

items.stem: Which of the following statements about angular momentum and equilibrium is correct?
items.answer: If no external torque acts, the angular momentum of a system is conserved.
items.markingKey: (b) Correct: "If no external torque acts, the angular momentum of a system is conserved." The other three are false.
options: An ice skater spins slower when she pulls her arms in.
If no external torque acts, the angular momentum of a system is conserved.
Angular momentum is conserved only when no external force acts, even if there is a torque.
A couple produces translation without rotation.

items.stem: What is a couple? Give an everyday example.
items.answer: Two equal and opposite forces with different lines of action; e.g. turning a steering wheel or a bottle cap.
items.markingKey: Definition (1 mark); example (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The angular momentum of a planet about the Sun is conserved.
Reason (R): The gravitational force on the planet is central and exerts no torque about the Sun.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Harpreet, an ice skater, spins at 2 rev s⁻¹ with arms stretched (moment of inertia 2.5 kg m²). On pulling the arms in, the moment of inertia becomes 1.25 kg m². Find the new rate of spin.
items.markingKey: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ ⇒ n₂ = I₁n₁/I₂ = 2.5 × 2/1.25 = 4.00 rev s⁻¹.

items.stem: A metre stick is balanced on a knife edge at its centre (the 50 cm mark). A 30 g mass hangs at the 15 cm mark. Where must a 25 g mass be hung to balance the stick?
A uniform plank of length 6 m and weight 500 N rests on two supports A and B at its ends. A boy of weight 300 N stands 3.6 m from A. Find the reactions at A and B.
A particle of mass 2 kg moves with speed 5 m s⁻¹ in a circle of radius 0.5 m. Find the magnitude of its angular momentum about the centre.
Riya, an ice skater, spins at 1 rev s⁻¹ with arms stretched (moment of inertia 3.6 kg m²). On pulling the arms in, the moment of inertia becomes 1.44 kg m². Find the new rate of spin.
items.markingKey: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ ⇒ n₂ = I₁n₁/I₂ = 3.6 × 1/1.44 = 2.50 rev s⁻¹.

items.stem: Why does an ice skater spin faster when she pulls her arms close to her body?
items.answer: Pulling arms in reduces I; with no external torque, L = Iω is constant, so ω increases.
items.markingKey: Conservation of L (1 mark); I decreases ⇒ ω increases (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A couple can be replaced by a single force.
Reason (R): A couple has zero resultant force.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false; R is true (a single force cannot have zero resultant and non-zero torque).
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A metre stick is balanced on a knife edge at its centre (the 50 cm mark). A 25 g mass hangs at the 30 cm mark. Where must a 20 g mass be hung to balance the stick?

A 3 m long ladder weighing 25 kg leans on a frictionless wall. Its feet rest on the floor 1 m from the wall. Find the reaction forces of the wall and the floor. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²; weight acts at the middle of the ladder)
items.answer: Wall: 43.3 N (horizontal); floor: 249 N at 80° to the horizontal
items.markingKey: Height of top = √(3² − 1²) = 2.83 m (1). Moments about the foot: F₁ × 2.83 = 245 × 0.5 ⇒ F₁ = 43.3 N (2). Floor: vertical 245 N, horizontal (friction) 43.3 N; resultant 249 N (2).

items.stem: A 5 m long ladder weighing 15 kg leans on a frictionless wall. Its feet rest on the floor 2 m from the wall. Find the reaction forces of the wall and the floor. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²; weight acts at the middle of the ladder)
items.answer: Wall: 32.1 N (horizontal); floor: 150 N at 77.7° to the horizontal
items.markingKey: Height of top = √(5² − 2²) = 4.58 m (1). Moments about the foot: F₁ × 4.58 = 147 × 1 ⇒ F₁ = 32.1 N (2). Floor: vertical 147 N, horizontal (friction) 32.1 N; resultant 150 N (2).

items.stem: Dev, an ice skater, spins at 1 rev s⁻¹ with arms stretched (moment of inertia 5 kg m²). On pulling the arms in, the moment of inertia becomes 2.5 kg m². Find the new rate of spin.
items.markingKey: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ ⇒ n₂ = I₁n₁/I₂ = 5 × 1/2.5 = 2.00 rev s⁻¹.

items.stem: The moment of inertia of a thin ring about its axis is
items.markingKey: (c) I(thin ring about its axis) = MR².
options: MR²/2
2MR²/3
MR²
2MR²/5

items.stem: Write the rotational analogues of mass, force, linear momentum and Newton's second law.
items.answer: Moment of inertia I, torque τ, angular momentum L, τ = Iα.
items.markingKey: Each pair ½ mark.

items.stem: Show that the rate of change of angular momentum of a particle is equal to the torque acting on it.
items.markingKey: l = r × p (1); dl/dt = (dr/dt × p) + (r × dp/dt) (2); first term v × mv = 0, second r × F = τ (2).

items.stem: A torque of 0.5 N m acts on a ring of mass 10 kg and radius 25 cm, free to rotate about its axis. Find its angular acceleration.

Shreya spins a potter's wheel (a uniform disc of mass 2 kg and radius 30 cm) up to 20 rad s⁻¹ and lets it go. Friction brings it to rest uniformly in 20 s.
(i) Find the moment of inertia. (ii) Find the angular deceleration. (iii) Find the frictional torque. (iv) Find the number of revolutions before it stops.
items.markingKey: (i) ½MR² (1). (ii) α = ω/t (1). (iii) τ = Iα (1). (iv) θ = ½ωt = 200 rad ÷ 2π (1).

items.stem: A cord of negligible mass is wound round the rim of a flywheel (treat as a ring) of mass 40 kg and radius 40 cm. A steady pull of 50 N is applied on the cord. The flywheel is mounted on a horizontal axle with frictionless bearings. Find (i) the angular acceleration, (ii) the work done by the pull when 2 m of cord is unwound and (iii) the angular speed then.
items.markingKey: (i) I = MR² = 6.4 kg m²; τ = FR = 20 N m; α = τ/I = 3.13 rad s⁻² (1). (ii) W = F × l = 100 J (1). (iii) ½Iω² = W ⇒ ω = 5.59 rad s⁻¹ (1).

items.stem: Find the radius of gyration of a solid sphere about a diameter, if R = 30 cm.

The angular speed of a motor wheel is increased from 1200 rpm to 3000 rpm in 5 s. (i) What is its angular acceleration, assuming it to be uniform? (ii) How many revolutions does the wheel make during this time?
items.markingKey: (i) ω₁ = 126, ω₂ = 314 rad s⁻¹; α = (ω₂ − ω₁)/t = 37.7 rad s⁻² (1.5). (ii) θ = ½(ω₁ + ω₂)t = 1100 rad = 175 rev (1.5).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about moment of inertia is correct?
items.answer: The radius of gyration k is given by I = Mk².
items.markingKey: (a) Correct: "The radius of gyration k is given by I = Mk²." The other three are false.
options: The radius of gyration k is given by I = Mk².
Moment of inertia is a vector quantity.
Moment of inertia depends only on the mass of the body.
The radius of gyration of a body is always equal to its geometrical radius.

items.stem: Two discs of moments of inertia 2 kg m² and 5 kg m² are on a common axis. The first rotates at 40 rad s⁻¹ and the second at 5 rad s⁻¹ in the same sense. They are brought into contact face to face and rotate together. Find the common angular speed and the loss of kinetic energy. Where does this energy go?
items.answer: 15.0 rad s⁻¹; loss 875 J (to heat by friction)
items.markingKey: No external torque: I₁ω₁ + I₂ω₂ = (I₁ + I₂)ω ⇒ ω = 15.0 rad s⁻¹ (2). KE before 1662.5 J, after 788 J; loss 875 J (2), dissipated by friction between the discs (1).

items.stem: A cord of negligible mass is wound round the rim of a flywheel (treat as a ring) of mass 25 kg and radius 20 cm. A steady pull of 50 N is applied on the cord. The flywheel is mounted on a horizontal axle with frictionless bearings. Find (i) the angular acceleration, (ii) the work done by the pull when 1 m of cord is unwound and (iii) the angular speed then.
items.markingKey: (i) I = MR² = 1 kg m²; τ = FR = 10 N m; α = τ/I = 10.0 rad s⁻² (1). (ii) W = F × l = 50 J (1). (iii) ½Iω² = W ⇒ ω = 10.0 rad s⁻¹ (1).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The moment of inertia of a body is fixed and does not depend on the axis.
Reason (R): Moment of inertia depends on mass distribution about the axis.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false; R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

items.stem: A flywheel of moment of inertia 4 kg m² rotates at 600 rpm. Find its rotational kinetic energy.

items.stem: Why does a ring have a greater moment of inertia than a disc of the same mass and radius?
items.answer: All the mass of the ring is at distance R from the axis; much of the disc's mass is nearer the axis.
items.markingKey: I = Σmr² (1 mark); comparison (1 mark).

items.stem: Why are flywheels made with most of their mass at the rim?
items.answer: A large moment of inertia resists changes in angular speed and smooths out the motion.
items.markingKey: Mass at rim ⇒ large I (1 mark); resists change in ω (1 mark).

items.stem: Find the radius of gyration of a thin rod about a perpendicular axis through its centre, if L = 20 cm.
Show that the work done by a constant torque τ in rotating a body through an angle θ is τθ, and that the power is τω.
items.markingKey: dW = F ds = F r dθ = τ dθ (2); integrate (1); P = dW/dt = τω (2).

items.stem: A torque of 5 N m acts on a ring of mass 10 kg and radius 20 cm, free to rotate about its axis. Find its angular acceleration.
items.markingKey: I = MR² = 0.4 kg m²; α = τ/I = 5/0.4 = 12.5 rad s⁻².

items.stem: A diver performs somersaults by curling up during the dive. Explain the physics.
items.answer: Curling reduces the moment of inertia, so the angular speed increases as angular momentum is conserved.
items.markingKey: L = Iω constant (1 mark); smaller I ⇒ larger ω (1 mark).

items.stem: Ishita, an ice skater, spins at 1.5 rev s⁻¹ with arms stretched (moment of inertia 5 kg m²). On pulling the arms in, the moment of inertia becomes 3.75 kg m². Find the new rate of spin.
items.markingKey: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ ⇒ n₂ = I₁n₁/I₂ = 5 × 1.5/3.75 = 2.00 rev s⁻¹.
